results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You should keep your business tax records for the period required by the IRS’s period‑of‑limitations rules and, in a few cases, for a fixed number of years after a tax becomes due or is paid.

* **General tax‑return records** – Keep any records that support an item of income or a deduction on a return until the period of limitation for that return expires. The usual period is **three (3) years** from the date the return is filed; for some situations it can be longer, up to **six (6) years** (e.g., if you omitted more than 25 % of gross income) or **not limited** (e.g., fraudulent returns). These limitations govern how long the IRS can challenge the return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least four (4) years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* **Asset and depreciation records** – Keep records relating to property (machinery, equipment, real estate, etc.) until the period of limitation expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. These records support depreciation, basis calculations, and gains/losses on sale. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* **Refund claims** – If you file a claim for a refund, you must generally file the claim **within three (3) years** from the date you filed the original return **or** **two (2) years** from the date you paid the tax, whichever is later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)  

* **Other records** – Keep copies of all filed tax returns, supporting documents such as invoices, receipts, and bank statements, and any other records needed for tax purposes until the applicable limitation period ends. If a record is no longer needed for tax purposes, don’t discard it until you verify whether another law (e.g., insurance, credit) requires longer retention. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several concrete reasons that are spelled out in the IRS guidance:

1. **Monitor the progress of your business** – Good records let you see which products or services are selling, which expenses are rising, and what changes you might need to make to improve performance. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
2. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets are built entirely from the records you keep; they are required for dealing with banks, creditors, and for internal decision‑making. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
3. **Support the entries in your books and on your tax return** – The IRS requires that you have supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, bank deposit slips, canceled checks, etc.) that prove the amounts you report. If the IRS audits you, these records enable you to explain the items reported and avoid penalties. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
4. **Maintain compliance with employment and other federal taxes** – If you have employees you must keep employment‑tax records for at least four years from the due or paid date, and you must keep records for other taxes (e.g., excise, self‑employment) as required. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
5. **Meet statutory record‑keeping periods** – The IRS sets periods of limitation (typically three to six years) during which records must be available to prove income or deductions; once those periods expire, you may dispose of them only if no other requirement (e.g., insurance or creditor) demands longer retention. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

In short, keeping business records keeps you in compliance with tax law, protects you in the event of an audit, supplies the information you need to run the business, and satisfies other legal and financial reporting obligations.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
**Which accounting method should you use?**

The right method depends on a few facts about your business.  
Use the rules below to decide.

| Condition | Suggested method | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **No inventory, cash‑only receipts, and only small amounts of receivables** | **Cash method** | The cash method records income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them, which is much simpler for a business that never holds inventory. This is the common choice for many sole proprietors and small businesses. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You keep inventory (goods for sale, raw materials, work‑in‑process, or finished products)** | **Accrual method** | Inventory requires “accrual” accounting so that income and expenses match the period in which the inventory is sold. If you are not a “small‑business taxpayer” (average gross receipts > $31 million over the past three years), you *must* use accrual for inventory. Small‑business taxpayers may still use the cash method, treating inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You want a mix but still need to show income clearly** | **Combination method** | You can combine cash and accrual for different items, but you must use the same method for all income (and similarly for all expenses). If inventory is involved, the portion of accounting that covers inventory must be accrual. Also, if you use cash for revenue but accrual for expenses—or vice‑versa—you are limited to the cash method for the whole business. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You are a new owner filing your FIRST return** | Pick your method now | Whichever method you choose with your first Schedule C (Form 1040) becomes your “chosen method” and must be used consistently for all future returns unless IRS approval is obtained. To change it later, you must file Form 3115 (Advance Consent or Automatic Procedure) and may have to pay a fee. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You think about changing later** | **Plan ahead** | If you anticipate needing a different method in the future, decide now and keep detailed, consistent records so the change can be approved more easily. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |

**How to determine if you’re a “small‑business taxpayer”**

| Requirement | How to calculate | Cut‑off |
|---|---|---|
| Average gross receipts for the prior 3 years (adjusted for inflation) | Sum the receipts for those years, divide by 3 | ≤ $31 million | 
| Not a tax‑shelter entity (as defined in IRC § 448(d)(3)) | Verify the business structure | — | 
| If the business has existed for < 3 years, use the actual existence period for the average calculation | (See Pub. 538) | — | 
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**Practical Tips**

* **If you have inventory but still want simplicity** – treat inventory items as “non‑incidental materials” only if you are a small‑business taxpayer. This keeps you on the cash method while meeting inventory reporting needs. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
* **If you keep inventory and are a larger business** – you must keep an inventory list, and the audit trail for each item, and report sales and purchases under the accrual method. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
* **Keep consistent records** – Every method requires that your books and the way you calculate taxable income match. Inconsistent treatment can trigger an audit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
* **Changing your method** – File Form 3115. If you qualify for the automatic change procedure (e.g., a small‑business, “cash to accrual” for inventory), you get approval without an IRS request. Otherwise, submit an advance (Form 3115) and possibly a user fee. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

---

**Bottom line**

1. **No inventory → Cash method** (unless you’re a very large business, see small‑business definition).  
2. **Inventory required → Accrual method** (unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer and can treat inventory as non‑incidental materials).  
3. **Special cases** → Combination method, but keep it consistent and note the IRS rules.  
4. **First return** → Pick and keep it. Changing it later requires Form 3115.

Follow these guidelines and refer to the cited segments for full rules and forms.

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
You can check your workplace for hazards by following a structured, step‑by‑step process that OSHA’s Small Business Safety and Health Handbook recommends:

1. **Plan a routine self‑inspection**  
   • Schedule regular inspections of all work areas, equipment, and processes.  
   • Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists as a starting point, choosing the sections that match your business’s activities and then expanding over time.  
   • Record what you find, noting any hazards you see or suspect.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Identify, assess, and control hazards**  
   • After completing a checklist, combine its results with injury/illness records, worker training logs, and maintenance or incident reports to see where problems appear.  
   • Use this information to decide which hazards need control measures and how to keep them safe.  
   • Verify that any controls you install remain effective by re‑checking them during subsequent inspections.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Incorporate a safety‑and‑health program**  
   • Treat hazard identification as a core element of your program, as OSHA’s recommended practices describe: “hazard identification and assessment.”  
   • Make hazard checks an ongoing part of daily work and worker conversations.  
   → [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

4. **Take advantage of free resources**  
   • If you need help figuring out whether a hazard is regulated or how to control it, contact an OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program.  Consultants can visit at no cost and guide your entire hazard‑identification and control process.  
   • Also, OSHA publishes safety and health program checklists and self‑evaluation tools on its website.  
   → [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

5. **Document and review**  
   • Keep a written safety and health program that lists the hazards you’ve found, the controls you’ve put in place, and the schedule for re‑inspection.  
   • Update and revise the program whenever new hazards appear or conditions change.  
   → [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)  

By regularly inspecting, recording findings, using the checklist as a baseline, and leveraging OSHA consultation services, you can systematically spot and eliminate workplace hazards.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash‑method accounting**

* You report income in the tax year you actually receive the money (or when it is constructively received).  
* You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay the cash outlay.  
* It is the simplest method and is often chosen by sole proprietors who don’t keep inventory.  
* Because cash receipts are the trigger, the method doesn’t automatically track what you owe or are owed.  

(Cited: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) “Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.”)

---

**Accrual‑method accounting**

* You report income in the year it is earned, even if the money is received later.  
* Expenses are deducted (or capitalized) in the year they are incurred, whether or not you have paid them.  The “all‑events” test and the “economic performance” test decide when an expense becomes deductible.  
* This method matches revenues with the expenses that produced them, giving a clearer picture of profitability.  
* If you keep inventory, you are generally required to use the accrual method for purchases and sales.  

(Cited: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) “If you use an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it… You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them… If an inventory is necessary… you must generally use an accrual method.”; [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally deduct or capitalize a business expense when both the all‑events test has been met and economic performance has occurred.”)

---

### Key differences at a glance

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **Income timing** | When cash (or equivalents) is received | When earned/economic performance occurs |
| **Expense timing** | When cash is paid | When the liability is fixed and can be reasonably determined |
| **Inventory requirement** | Not required unless you keep inventory | Required if you sell, purchase, or produce merchandise |
| **Tax reporting simplicity** | Easier to maintain, no need for inventory records | Requires more bookkeeping (e.g., accounts receivable, inventory, cost of goods sold) |
| **Matching principle** | Not automatically matched | Automatically matches revenues with related expenses |

(Cited: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) “You can deduct the expense in 2025 because all events that fix the fact of liability have occurred… economic performance occurred in that year.”)

---

### When to choose each

* **Cash** – Good for small businesses, farms, real‑estate rentals, or workers who want a quick, straightforward view of cash flow.  
* **Accrual** – Recommended for businesses that sell goods or services on credit, keep inventory, or need a more accurate analysis of profitability for lenders or investors.  

(Cited: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier…”; [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) “If an inventory is necessary… you must generally use an accrual method…”)

---

results.question: can i deduct business travel

Yes – the IRS allows ordinary and necessary business‑travel expenses to be deducted on your federal tax return.  
The segments give the specific types of expenses that qualify and the rules for each:

| Expense | What you can deduct | Key rules | Source |
|---------|---------------------|-----------|--------|
| **Transportation (air, train, bus, car)** between your home and a temporary work site | The full cost is deductible | Must be away from your tax home more than an ordinary day’s work and you need sleep or rest while away | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine, rides‑share, etc.** between airports/stations and hotels or between hotel and work location | Fares are deductible | Same “away from home” requirement as above | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Car or truck used for business** | You may use **actual expenses** or the **standard mileage rate** (70¢ per mile for 2025) | If you elect the standard rate you cannot claim actual expenses except for parking, tolls, and business‑related interest; you may still claim the business portion of loan interest | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Baggage and shipping** of luggage or sample/display material between work locations | Deductible | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Meals** during an overnight or otherwise extended business trip | You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging, or use the standard meal allowance; generally only 50 % of meal costs are deductible unless a special exception applies | Must meet the overnight/long‑trip test | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging** during a qualifying business trip | Deductible under the same rules as meals | Must be an overnight or long‑trip stay | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Cleaning (dry cleaning, laundry)** while traveling | Deductible | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Telephone** used for business while traveling | Deductible (all business calls, fax, etc.) | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips** paid on any travel expense | Deductible | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Reimbursement of employees** for any of the above travel expenses | Deductible | Depends on whether the reimbursement is under an accountable or non‑accountable plan | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
The executive summary is the short, one‑ or two‑paragraph overview that is written last. It tells the reader what the business intends to achieve and how it will get there. According to the guide, it should:

* **Briefly describe the business idea** – what you’re offering and why it matters.  
* **State the amount of capital you need** – how much money you’re seeking and what it will be used for.  
* **Explain how much money you have already invested** – the owner’s contribution or other equity.  
* **Outline a timeline of goals** – a short schedule of milestones you plan to hit.  

Because the executive summary is written after the main plan is complete, it can pull together the final figures and conclusions from the rest of the document. It is intentionally concise but should give the reader a clear snapshot of the plan’s purpose and key financial needs. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
**How to describe your target market**

1. **Define your market niche** – start by stating who your “best” customer is.  
   *Identify the group that will buy the most from you and the one that will be the easiest to serve.*  
   *Example:* “Our best customers are small‑to‑medium‑sized construction firms in the Midwest that need high‑strength, locally sourced steel bars.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Segment the customer base** by the dimensions that matter to your business.  
   - **Business markets:** industry, company size, location, product use/application.  
   - **Consumer markets:** age, gender, income level, geography, lifestyle, product benefits sought.  
   *Example:* “Within the construction sector, we target firms with annual revenues of $2‑$20 million located within 200 km of our plant.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Describe the customers’ key characteristics** – the traits that make them a good fit.  
   - Demographic facts (age, income, gender).  
   - Psychographic traits (values, buying motivations).  
   - Behavioral factors (purchase frequency, brand loyalty).  
   *Example:* “These firms value reliability, prefer a single‑supply partnership, and are willing to pay a premium for on‑time delivery.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate the market size and growth potential** – give numbers that show the opportunity.  
   - Use population or industry data, sales tax records, or industry reports.  
   - Provide an estimate of how many of those customers you can realistically reach.  
   *Example:* “The Midwestern construction steel market is $3 billion annually, growing 4 % per year; we project capturing 0.5 % of that in year 1, increasing to 1 % by year 3.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Show how much of the total market you plan to capture** – translate the percentage into revenue or units.  
   *Example:* “Capturing 0.5 % of a $3 billion market equals $15 million in sales in year 1.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

---

**Key take‑away terms**

| Term | Definition (from guide) |
|------|------------------------|
| **Target market** | The specific group of customers you are focused on serving. |
| **Segmentation** | Dividing a broad market into subgroups that share similar characteristics. |
| **Market niche** | A specialized segment where your product or service has a competitive advantage. |
| **Market size** | The total sales potential (in dollars or units) of a defined market. |
| **Market share** | The portion of the total market that you expect to capture. |

Follow this structure and use the data you gather (industry reports, census data, etc.) to fill in each bullet. This gives investors or readers a clear picture of *who* you serve, *why* they matter, and *how big* the opportunity is.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
**Answer**

Yes. Because your shop is a private business that serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove “readily achievable” barriers that prevent people who use wheelchairs from entering and using the business. 

* The ADA defines private businesses that provide goods or services to the public as *public accommodations* and makes them subject to compliance even if they were built before the law’s 1992 deadline [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
* The law specifically says that existing facilities are not exempted by “grandfather” provisions and that you must remove barriers that are *readily achievable* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
* An accessible entrance is the first requirement: you must have at least one accessible entrance (or provide an alternate accessible route) and, if it is a primary entrance, it must be available during business hours [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
* If furnishing a fully accessible entrance is not *readily achievable*, the ADA allows you to provide alternative means of service (e.g., home delivery or curb‑side service), but you still need to provide service to disabled customers in some other accessible way [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
* In addition, the entrance must lead to an “accessible route” that allows wheelchair users to move inside the shop, and sales or service counters should have a lowered portion no higher than 36 inches so that a wheelchair user can use them [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).

So, unless you can prove the required changes are *impractically difficult, expensive, or otherwise not readily achievable*, you must make your shop wheelchair‑accessible. If you find the required changes impractical, you must still provide the services in an accessible manner (e.g., alternative service or assistance).

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping only if you meet specific criteria.  You do not have to keep OSHA Form 300, 301 or 300A records if:

* **Your business had ten or fewer employees during every day of the last calendar year** (see 29 CFR 1904.1), or  
* **Your business is in a low‑hazard industry listed in 29 CFR 1904 Subpart B, Appendix A**.

If either of those conditions applies, you are partially exempt.  Otherwise you must maintain the usual OSHA injury‑recordkeeping records.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
You can protect your staff and make your place open to all customers by putting together two kinds of plans and following the concrete rules in the OSHA/ADA handbook.

---

## 1.  Keep employees safe – OSHA safety program

| What you must do | Where the rule comes from |
|------------------|---------------------------|
| **Create a written safety‑and‑health program** that shows management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification, hazard prevention, training, program evaluation, and communication. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Carry out regular workplace inspections** and fix hazards before they cause injury. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Keep all machinery and equipment clean, well‑maintained and properly guarded** and provide power‑shutdown switches within reach. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) |
| **Install guardrails, splash guards, lock‑out/tag‑out devices and emergency‑stop buttons** on machines. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) |
| **Keep walkways and aisles clear**—no holes, detours, or protruding clutter; at least 36 in. turn‑around space at corners; 36‑in. wide for wheelchair access if the business can accommodate that width. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) |
| **Post an emergency action plan** that lists key personnel, contact info, evacuation routes, medical assistance, and protects disabled workers. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=25), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=27) |
| **Train employees** on the hazards in their jobs and how to use the safety equipment. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=92) (training requirement in OSHA 1904) |
| **Keep records** (injury logs, training records, medical records) for at least five years. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

---

## 2.  Keep your premises accessible – ADA & “readily achievable” rules

| Feature | Specific requirement | Segment |
|---------|----------------------|---------|
| **Entrance** | No steps; if needed, a ramp with a maximum slope of **1:12**; handrails on sloping surfaces >1:20; doors 36 in. wide; hinges that provide at least 1½ in. clearance. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11), [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |

**How to write a business plan**

1. **Cover Page** – Include the company name, address, phone number, owners’ contact info, logo and the date of the plan.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  

2. **Executive Summary** – 1–2 paragraphs that preview the idea, the amount of money you need, how you will use it, and a brief schedule of goals.  Write this last so you can pull together the most current figures.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  

3. **Business Description** – Explain what your product or service is, the industry context, and the competitive advantage you will maintain.  Highlight any proprietary technology, patents, or trademarks you own or are pursuing.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)*  

4. **Market Analysis** – Detail the total market, target customers, competitors, and your marketing strategy.  Provide data on market size, growth trends, and your pricing/branding plans.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  

5. **Organization & Management** – Specify the legal form (sole‑prop, partnership, LLC, corporation), ownership percentages, key staff responsibilities, and any consultants.  Attach resumes and organizational charts if possible.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)*  

6. **Operations Plan** – Cover facilities, equipment, inventory, manufacturing or service delivery methods, and any regulatory requirements or licenses needed.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)*  

7. **Financial Plan** –  
   * **Sources & Uses of Funds** – Show the total cost of the project, working capital, equity injected, and debt planned.  Include a detailed worksheet of long‑term, intangible, and short‑term assets and the corresponding financing sources.  
     *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=21)*  
   * **Projected Statements** – Provide a three‑year income statement, cash‑flow projection, balance sheet, and break‑even analysis.  These should be based on market data and include assumptions and supporting notes.  
     *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)*  

8. **Appendices & Exhibits** – Attach resumes, contracts, purchase agreements, marketing research, and any other substantiating documents.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)*  

**How to set up accounting**

1. **Choose a legal structure & obtain an EIN** – If you’ll hire employees or pay excise taxes, get a federal Employer Identification Number.  Record this and any state registration.  
   *[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)*  

2. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – Keep all business income and expenses in this account and note the source of each deposit and check.  Use a checkbook that allows you to identify business income, personal funds, or loans.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*  

3. **Decide on a tax year and accounting method** –  
   * Pick a calendar‑year (Jan 1–Dec 31) or a fiscal‑year.  A new business can choose either when filing its first return.  
     *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)*  
   * Select a cash or accrual method (small businesses may use cash unless inventory is required).  The method must consistently show your income.  
     *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)*  

4. **Set up a bookkeeping system**  
   * **Single‑entry** – Keep a daily cash‑receipt book and a monthly cash‑receipt summary.  Suitable for very small businesses.  
   * **Double‑entry** – Use journals and ledgers; each transaction is recorded as a debit and a credit, ensuring the books balance

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) ?**  
- If you **hire employees** or if you must **pay federal excise tax**, you must obtain an EIN.  
- If you are a **sole proprietor with no employees**, you may **choose** to get an EIN instead of using your Social Security number; it is not required unless you have employees or other tax‑reporting obligations.  
  – The IRS also requires an EIN if you need to file pension or excise tax returns.  
  – An EIN can be applied for online (immediately), by fax (≈4 business days), or by mail (≈4 weeks before you need it).  
  – You should apply for an EIN early enough that you have it by the time you must file a return or make a tax deposit.  
  – If you do not receive it in time, you can still file your return and write “Applied for” next to the EIN field.  
  – Do not use your social‑security number on business returns if you have an EIN.  
  – The relevant rules appear in [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4), and [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

**What accounting method do you use, and does it “come with” the EIN?**  
- The **accounting method is not tied to having an EIN**; it is chosen when you file your first business income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040).  
- You may select one of the following primary methods:  
  1. **Cash method** – income is reported when received; expenses are deducted/​capitalized when paid.  
  2. **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned, even if not yet received; expenses are deducted/​capitalized when incurred.  
- A **combination method** (cash for some items, accrual for others) is allowed **only** if it “clearly shows your income.”  
- You must use the same method consistently for both income‑tax calculation and bookkeeping.  
- Certain situations (e.g., having inventory that is necessary to account for your income) require an accrual method unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer.  
- This choice is independent of whether you have an EIN; the EIN is simply a taxpayer identification number and does not dictate the accounting method.  
  – References: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) (detailed description of cash, accrual, and combination methods), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) (discussion of method choice at first filing), and [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) (rules for inventory and choosing an appropriate method).

**Bottom line:**  
- **Yes** you need an EIN if you have employees, pay federal excise tax, or file pension/excise returns; you may get one if you are a sole proprietor.  
- **No** the EIN forces a particular accounting method—you still select either cash, accrual, or an appropriate combination when you file your first return.

All OSHA injury and illness records—Forms 300, 301, and 300A—must be retained for **at least five years** from the date of injury or illness, or from the date of reporting, whichever is later. This retention period covers both the physical and an equivalent electronic storage system if you maintain an electronic record‑keeping system. The forms must be available for inspection by OSHA, but you are not required to submit them to OSHA electronically unless you fall under the specific filing thresholds (e.g., employers with 100 or more workers in high‑hazard industries).

To register a trademark you can go through either a state‑level or a federal‑level process.  
At the state level you file with your state’s Secretary of State office. At the federal level you file with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).  

* **State registration** – Contact the Secretary of State in South Dakota (or your respective state).  Call (605) 773‑2797 or visit https://sdsos.gov/.  
* **Federal registration** – Contact the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.  Call (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or visit www.uspto.gov.  

Before filing, consider searching the USPTO’s online trademark database to confirm the name or mark has not already been registered. This will help you avoid conflicts and increase the chance your application is approved.

results.question: what health insurance plan should i buy for my staff
results.answer:
A small‑business owner who wants to give staff health insurance should consider a **group hospitalization and medical insurance plan** (often called a group health plan).  This is the type of coverage that the IRS allows a business to deduct as a business expense and that provides employees with cure‑and‑care benefits.

- The handbook lists **“group hospitalization and medical insurance for employees, including long‑term care insurance”** as an eligible deductible expense for a small business [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37).  

If you want to offer a more comprehensive package that also helps employees with chronic or long‑term care needs, you can add long‑term care insurance to the group plan.  Such coverage can be included in the overall group health policy or offered as a supplemental benefit.

In short, buying a **group medical (hospitalization) insurance plan—optionally with long‑term care coverage added—** is the health‑insurance solution the handbook recommends for small‑biz employees.
